summary: Describes OAuth client authentication using mutual TLS with X.509 certificates, and certificate-bound access and refresh tokens. Authorization servers can bind tokens to the client's certificate, and protected resources can check that binding, so stolen tokens are less useful.

plainLanguage.summary: OAuth 2.0 clients normally prove who they are with a shared secret, and an access token normally works for whoever holds it. RFC 8705 adds two options: a client can authenticate with a TLS client certificate, and the authorization server can tie an access token to that certificate so only the client holding the matching private key can use the token.

questions: how do certificate bound access tokens work
subtitle: Lets an OAuth client authenticate with a TLS certificate and ties access tokens to that certificate.

tldr.problem: An OAuth access token can be used by anyone who obtains it, and the shared secret a client normally uses to authenticate to the authorization server is a weaker credential.
tldr.mechanism: The client authenticates with an X.509 certificate during the TLS handshake, and the authorization server binds the issued access token to a hash of that certificate. The protected resource compares the hash with the certificate the client presents on its own TLS connection.
tldr.outcome: A stolen access token is useless without the matching private key. The RFC compares this with OAuth 2.0 Token Binding and notes that mutual TLS can be built now because TLS servers and tools already support it.

facts.label: Binding hash
facts.value: SHA-256 over the DER encoding of the certificate

today: RFC 8705 is a Proposed Standard, published in February 2020. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so it is still the published specification for these two mechanisms.

sections.title: Two Security Options for OAuth Clients
sections.content:
The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749) lets a third-party client application obtain delegated access to protected resources. The client gets an access token from an authorization server and then presents that token when it calls a protected resource such as an HTTPS API. The protected resource validates the token before it authorizes the request. It can do that locally when the token is self-contained and cryptographically secured, or it can call the authorization server to learn the state of the token and its metainformation.

This RFC adds two optional security mechanisms built on client-certificate mutual TLS. The first is client authentication at the authorization server, described in Section 2. The second is certificate-bound access tokens, described in Section 3, where the token itself records the hash of the client certificate so a protected resource can check that the same certificate was presented. The two mechanisms are complementary but do not have to be deployed together.

The RFC also notes that the mutual-TLS methods apply to other endpoints that use client authentication, such as introspection, revocation and the backchannel authentication endpoint. New client metadata parameters support both mechanisms, and the authorization server can obtain that metadata through the Dynamic Client Registration Protocol (RFC 7591).
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives OAuth clients two extra ways to prove who they are. A client can use a TLS certificate instead of a shared secret, and an access token can be tied to that certificate so a stolen token does not work on its own.

sections.title: Mutual TLS Client Authentication
sections.content:
The authorization server decides, per client, whether mutual TLS is required, based on its own policy or configuration for that client. The TLS connection between the client and the authorization server MUST have been established or re-established with mutual-TLS X.509 certificate authentication, which in contemporary TLS versions means the client sends its Certificate and CertificateVerify messages during the handshake. Every such request MUST include the client_id parameter, so the server can identify the client independently of the certificate contents and locate the client's configuration. The server then enforces the binding between client and certificate. If no certificate is presented, or the one presented does not match what is expected for that client_id, the server returns an OAuth 2.0 error response with the invalid_client error code.

Two methods are defined. In the PKI method (tls_client_auth) the server validates the certificate chain and matches one expected subject: the certificate must carry the single subject distinguished name or the single subject alternative name configured for that client. The client MUST use exactly one of tls_client_auth_subject_dn, tls_client_auth_san_dns, tls_client_auth_san_uri, tls_client_auth_san_ip or tls_client_auth_san_email. Whether and how revocation status is checked is a deployment decision. A client can rotate its certificate without changing anything at the server by getting a new certificate with the same subject from a trusted certificate authority.

In the self-signed method (self_signed_tls_client_auth) the client registers its certificates through jwks or points to them with jwks_uri, and the server does not validate the certificate chain at all. The client is authenticated if the certificate it presented matches one of the certificates configured or registered for that client. This allows mutual TLS without maintaining a public key infrastructure, and a client that publishes a jwks_uri can rotate its certificates without changing data at the authorization server.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization server decides, for each client, whether a TLS client certificate is required. The client sends its certificate during the TLS handshake and also sends its client ID, so the server knows which client to check the certificate against. Two methods exist: one checks the certificate chain against a trusted authority, the other only checks the certificate against a list the client registered earlier.

sections.title: Certificate-Bound Access Tokens
sections.content:
When the client uses mutual TLS on the connection to the token endpoint, the authorization server is able to bind the issued access token to the client certificate. The binding has to be readable by the protected resource, so the RFC defines two ways to carry it: embed the certificate hash in the token itself, or return it in a token introspection response. Because the binding travels separately from the client authentication, mutual TLS during protected resource access serves purely as a proof of possession.

For an access token represented as a JSON Web Token (RFC 7519), the certificate hash SHOULD be carried in the cnf claim as the x5t#S256 member. That value is a base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the DER encoding of the X.509 certificate. The base64url value MUST omit all trailing = pad characters and MUST NOT include line breaks, whitespace or other additional characters. For token introspection (RFC 7662) the same cnf structure with the x5t#S256 member is a top-level member of the introspection response JSON.

When the client uses the token, the request MUST be made over a mutually authenticated TLS connection using the same certificate that was used at the token endpoint. The protected resource MUST obtain the client certificate from its TLS implementation layer and MUST verify that it matches the certificate associated with the access token. If they do not match, the resource access attempt MUST be rejected with an HTTP 401 status code and the invalid_token error code.

Because a TLS client only presents a certificate when the server asks for one during the handshake, the protected resource must know in advance that mutual TLS is to be used. The access token itself cannot decide this, because from the TLS point of view it is application data that is only exchanged after the handshake has completed, while the certificate request happens during the handshake. This document makes no provision for TLS 1.2 renegotiation or TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization server can record the hash of the client certificate inside the access token. When the client calls the protected resource, it presents that certificate again during the TLS handshake. The resource computes the hash of the presented certificate and compares it with the one in the token. If they differ, the resource refuses the request with an error.

sections.title: Public Clients and Bound Tokens
sections.content:
Certificate-bound access tokens do not require mutual-TLS client authentication. A public client, which has no authentication credentials associated with its client_id, can use them on its own. The authorization server configures its TLS stack in the same manner as for the self-signed method, so that it does not verify that the certificate presented during the handshake was signed by a trusted certificate authority. Individual instances of the client create a self-signed certificate for mutual TLS with both the authorization server and the resource server. The authorization server does not use the certificate to authenticate the client at the OAuth layer, but binds the issued access token to the certificate whose private key the client has proven it holds. The token can then only be used by the client that possesses the certificate and the corresponding private key, using them to negotiate mutual TLS on connections to the resource server.

When the authorization server issues a refresh token to such a client, it SHOULD also bind the refresh token to the respective certificate and check the binding when the refresh token is presented to get new access tokens. The implementation details of that binding are at the discretion of the authorization server.
sections.plainLanguage: A client that has no password of its own can still get a bound token. It makes its own certificate, and the authorization server ties the token to that certificate. Only the client instance holding the matching private key can then use the token.

sections.title: Separate Endpoints for Mutual TLS
sections.content:
The process of negotiating client-certificate mutual TLS involves the TLS server requesting a certificate from the client, because the client does not provide one unsolicited. Even where a server is configured so that client certificates are optional, the act of requesting one can produce undesirable behaviour in some clients. This is particularly true of web browsers used as TLS clients, which typically present the end user with an intrusive certificate selection interface when the server requests a certificate.

An authorization server that supports both mutual-TLS clients and conventional clients MAY isolate the server-side mutual-TLS behaviour so that only clients intending to use it are affected. The new metadata parameter mtls_endpoint_aliases supports this. It is an optional JSON object containing alternative authorization server endpoints, such as token_endpoint, revocation_endpoint and introspection_endpoint. A client that intends to do mutual TLS MUST use the alias URL of an endpoint within mtls_endpoint_aliases when one is present, in preference to the endpoint URL of the same name at the top level of the authorization server metadata. When an endpoint is not present in the alias object, the client uses the conventional endpoint URL. In the example metadata given in the RFC, the alias endpoints use a different host than their conventional counterparts, which allows the server, through the TLS server_name extension or through genuinely distinct hosts, to differentiate its TLS behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for a client certificate can upset web browsers, which show the user a certificate selection box. A server can therefore publish a second set of endpoint addresses for clients that want to use a certificate, and keep the ordinary addresses for everyone else.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
An authorization server that supports mutual-TLS client authentication alongside other authentication methods or public clients would make mutual TLS optional, allowing the handshake to continue after the server requests a client certificate but the client does not send one. To support the self-signed method alone, the server would configure its TLS stack so that it does not verify whether the certificate presented during the handshake is signed by a trusted certificate authority. It may also host the token endpoint and other endpoints that require client authentication on a separate host name or port, to prevent unintended impact on the TLS behaviour of its other endpoints, such as the authorization endpoint, and to keep the certificate request away from conventional clients.

The resource server relies on the authorization server for client authentication, so it does not need to validate the trust chain of the client certificate in any of the methods defined here. It would configure its TLS stack in the same way as the server. It still has to obtain the client certificate and compare it with the binding carried by the token.

Because an access token is bound to a specific client certificate, the same certificate must be used for mutual TLS on protected resource access, and access tokens are invalidated when a client updates its certificate. That is handled like an expired access token: the client requests a new access token, typically with a refresh token, and retries the protected resource request. Binding of access tokens issued directly from the authorization endpoint through the implicit grant flow is explicitly out of scope, so implementations wanting certificate-bound tokens should use grant types where the client makes the access token request directly to the token endpoint, such as the authorization code and refresh token grants. An authorization server or resource server MAY terminate TLS at a load balancer, reverse proxy or other intermediary; how the client certificate metadata is communicated securely to the application server in that case is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The server that checks the token does not have to decide whether the certificate came from a trusted authority. It only compares the certificate it received with the one recorded in the token. A client that replaces its certificate must get a new token, because the old one no longer matches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Refresh tokens are already bound to the client by RFC 6749, which requires the authorization server to bind refresh tokens to the client to which they were issued and requires confidential clients to authenticate when presenting one. Refresh tokens for clients using the mutual-TLS methods are therefore indirectly certificate-bound through the client ID and the associated requirement for certificate-based authentication to the authorization server. Section 4 describes certificate-bound refresh tokens issued to public clients.

The thumbprint binding uses a cryptographic hash of the certificate. It relies on the hash function having sufficient second-preimage resistance, so that finding or creating a different certificate with the same hash output is not feasible. SHA-256 was used because it meets that requirement while being widely available. The RFC also notes that community knowledge about algorithm strength and feasible attacks can change suddenly, and that a document about security is a point-in-time statement.

With the PKI method, an attacker could try to impersonate a client using a certificate with the same subject issued by a different certificate authority that the authorization server trusts. To cope with that threat the server SHOULD accept only a limited number of certificate authorities as trust anchors, whose certificate issuance policy meets its security requirements. That relies on the client and server agreeing out of band on the set of trust anchors the server uses to create and validate certificate chains. Parsing and validating X.509 certificates and certificate chains is complex, and implementation mistakes have previously exposed security vulnerabilities. Implementors SHOULD therefore use an established and well-tested X.509 library for validation and SHOULD NOT attempt to write their own X.509 certificate validation procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Trust only a small number of certificate authorities, so that an attacker cannot get a certificate with the same name from a different one. And use a tested library to check certificates, because writing that check from scratch is a known source of security bugs.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content: In TLS versions prior to 1.3, the client's certificate is sent unencrypted in the initial handshake, and third parties can potentially use it to monitor, track and correlate client activity. This is likely of little concern for clients that act on behalf of a significant number of end users, because individual user activity will not be discernible amidst the client activity as a whole. Clients that act on behalf of a single end user, such as a native application on a mobile device, should use TLS version 1.3 whenever possible, or consider the potential privacy implications of using mutual TLS on earlier versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Before TLS 1.3 the client sends its certificate in the clear, so anyone watching the connection can see which client it is. A client that represents one person should use TLS 1.3 where it can.
